# Slate

everything a film knows lives in its own folder, so any agent in any session can pick up exactly where the last one

A format is a template in Slate's `formats/` folder. It sets the runtime, aspect and size, frame rate, pace, structure,
loudness target, caption defaults, per-platform safe zones and the default budget. `slate new --format <name>` copies
its values into film.json, which is then the one source of the film's clock and size. Nothing downstream assumes a

# slate-motion

Motion is where a film feels made by hand or made by a template. Slate's films earned their motion the hard way: a
motion law measured from reference films and the product's own tokens, a catalogue of every glitch that shipped to a
review and why, and a character spec rewritten after "it's super glitchy". This skill carries all of it, generalized
for any brand.

The law is data, the kit enforces it, and a gate checks it:
- the brand's **motion law** lives in its pack (`motion` in brand.json, written at onboarding);
- the Remotion kit moves things only by the law's names and exact-endpoint eases, and records every move;
- `slate emit-events` writes each act's motion trace, and `slate qa motion` checks it.

## 1. The north star and the bar

- **The Browser Company's craft and warmth** is the north star: motion that feels hand-made, where every move has one
  reason and lands with its sound. Borrow the feeling, never their brand; express it inside the brand's own tokens.
- **The visionary bar:** beautiful enough to make someone cry. One signature moment per act; correct but ordinary
  isn't enough (slate-story sets the moment, this skill stages it).
- **Intentionality:** one carrier per act, one idea per beat, every move tied to the voice's word or to the idea.
  Fewer, better moves. Stillness is part of the design.

| move | rest-to-rest moves: camera push, pull and truck; carries | starts and ends at rest |
| relayout | short make-room re-layouts (0.4 s or less) | quick, soft |

# slate-story

The story is data. One hand-edited file, `script/script.json`, holds every act and shot: what the voice says, what's on
screen, what the picture does, and where every claim comes from. `slate script build` checks it through the script
gates and writes the storyboard and a readable SCRIPT.md, and it refuses to write anything while a gate fails. Nothing
downstream is typed by hand: shot lengths, timecodes and frames all come from this file and the voice's real reads.

This skill covers stages 2 (truth), 3 (treatment and script) and 5 (timing) of the production. The front door (the
slate skill) has already made the film folder and the brief.

## 1. Truth first

Before a line is written, know what's true and who says so.
- The **brand's truth** (from onboarding): its claim authority, sources, approved claims, never-claim list, banned
  words and sample data.
- The **film's truth pack**, `brief/truth.json`: the sources this film relies on, each pinned (a commit, a retrieval
  date or a hash), the researched claims that cite them, what this film never claims, and its sample data.
- The product's own code, read in place at a pinned commit, is the only product truth: it wins over docs, demos,
  prototypes and older films. The owner's rulings win over the code for what's claimed.

Every claim and every number said or shown must be on the brand's approved list or cite a pinned source. Autonomous
films use approved claims only. Research method and templates: [truth](references/truth.md). The rules every frame and
line obeys: [truth packs](references/truth-packs.md).

## 2. The treatment

For anything longer than a short ad, write a treatment before the script: the idea as a reframe, why this runtime, act
by act, the emotional arc, one signature moment per act, the voice and the look and the sound in a line each, what the

When the script builds clean (and the treatment, the truth pack and the voice shortlist are ready), stop. The

isn't approved, the look test. Say what's ready, where it is (SCRIPT.md, the truth pack, the casting reel), and what
each decision is. Record the owner's calls on the draft (trims, keeps, confirmations) as numbered decisions in the
tracker, with their words.

## Rules that hold everywhere

- One hand-edited source. Never edit storyboard.json, SCRIPT.md or the timing files; change script.json and rebuild.
- Nothing is invented: every UI element, word and number maps to a citation (truth packs).
- No invented testimonials or customer quotes presented as real; quotes carry who said them and a pinned source.
- Runtime stays within 10% of the target unless the requester asks otherwise or you justify it in the tracker.
- The picture can be restaged freely by builders; the words, beats and timing are the script's.

# Truth research: sources you can pin and cite

A film is only as trustworthy as the sources behind it. Truth research finds what's actually true about the product
and the brand, pins each source so it can be re-checked, and records who rules on what's claimed.

## The order of authority

1. **The owner's rulings** on what's claimed. A feature can exist in the code and still be ruled out for the film
   ("that's not true" means it doesn't appear).
2. **The product's code**, read in place at a pinned commit and cited `path:line`. It wins over everything below.
3. **The brand's website, live product pages, public demos and guidelines**, read and cited with the date.
4. **Docs, prototypes, demos and older films**: layout references only. They drift: names change, numbers move,
   features are retired. When they disagree with the code, the code wins; when a product demo's wording disagrees with
   the product's code, the code wins.

For a brand the owner doesn't own, the brand's **claim authority** (a named person there) rules on claims and brand use.

**Nothing is invented**: every UI element, word and number in the film maps to a citation in the truth pack. A concept
screen (something not built) needs the requester's explicit sign-off and a visible "concept" treatment. The rules that
follow from this are in [truth packs](truth-packs.md).

## Pinning a source

Every source in `brief/truth.json` has an id and a pin: a commit, a retrieval date or a SHA-256. A claim cites a pinned
source by id, with where in it (`path:line`, a page, a section). A number with no pinned source doesn't go in the film.

```json
{
 "claim_authority": "the person who rules on this brand's claims",
 "sources": [
  {"id": "app", "title": "The product's source", "pin": "commit 3f2a9c1", "note": "read in place, never copied"},
  {"id": "site", "title": "The public website", "url": "https://example.com", "retrieved_at": "2026-09-30", "pin": "2026-09-30"}
 ],
 "claims": [
  {"id": "c1", "text": "Plans a week in one view", "source": "app", "where": "src/views/week.tsx:40"}
 ],
 "never_claim": ["works offline"],
 "sample_data": {"company": "an invented sample company, always labelled as sample data"}
}
```

## Reading company code

- Read it in place, on the machine that holds it, with read-only commands (`git show`, `git grep` at the pinned
  commit). Never copy it to another machine, into Slate, or into a prompt for a generator.
- Quote the exact copy the product uses (labels, statuses, limits) with `path:line`, and re-verify quotes before the
  build: a first pass once had to correct line numbers on about a hundred quotes.
- A voice brief or research note that quotes company code stays with the company's material; it never travels into a
  personal or public package.

## Templates

### Product truth

For a product film, write one product-truth document the builders work from:
- the pinned commit;
- the product in one paragraph;
- the journey order (how a person really goes through it);
- every screen the film shows, with its exact copy;
- the product's agent or character, if it has one;
- secondary views (partners, admins, settings);
- the product's own motion (its CSS easing tokens or its springs);
- the palette and type the film takes;
- **live versus not built**: what's shipped, what's stubbed or off by default (never shown as working);
- numbers and words to get exactly right;
- where the product disagrees with itself.

### Capability brief (for a product character or agent)

How it was checked; sources; what it knows; how it synthesizes and explains; what it suggests next; its guardrails;
**what is not true about it**; where this film differs from the product; and what the film uses. Every line carries a
source. Describe a character only with capabilities the owner treats as true.

### Reference analysis claims

When a film remakes or answers an earlier film, list every claim in the original that conflicts with the brand's
current website or product, and decide each with the claim authority before writing.

## Checking numbers

- Recheck an original's statistics against a current public source; cut or correct any that don't match.
- A figure from an older source that can't be verified goes to the claim authority before it's used.
- Percentiles, ranges and derived numbers are computed from the product's own model, not eyeballed.
- One company, one set of numbers: every shot that shows the sample reads from one sample-data record, so the same
  company never shows two different weeks.

lines as context so the reads flow as one narration, then cleans, paces and times them, and checks every take before

never decide.

replays offline in tests (`SLATE_FAKE_VENDORS=1`); `--live` spends.

## 1. The profile and the cloning policy

The brand's pack holds its voice profile (provider, voice id, model, settings, lexicon of brand words); a film pins

  themselves. An agent never does that verification.
- **Anyone else's voice** only as a real recording, never a clone, and never a public figure's.
- Autonomous agents may narrate with the owner's own clone; their films are still held for the owner.

- **Design** a new voice from a brief: `slate voice design --descripti

- Say only what the approved claims say. Sample numbers are always labelled as sample data.

# Casting: choosing a voice by ear

A casting shootout has several voices read the same lines, measures every take, and gives the owner a listening reel.
The owner chooses by ear; the measurements only filter out takes that fail and put the rest in a sensible order.

## Running a shootout

```
slate voice cast --voices <voice-id>,<voice-id>,<voice-id> --shots S01,S05
slate voice cast --text "<a line that matters>" --name opening-line
```

- Pick lines that matter: the opening line, a line with the brand's name, a line with a number, the emotional peak.
- Every candidate reads the same lines on the production model with the same settings.
- Each take is measured: pace (words a second), pauses at full stops and turns, pitch range, falling endings on
  statements, the noise floor, and whether Whisper hears every word, including each brand word said in full.
- The reel is level-matched (every take at the same loudness), labelled, and plays the takes one after another, so the
  owner compares voices, not volumes.
- A clone or a famous voice among the candidates is refused before anything is spent.

## Choosing

- **The owner picks by ear.** Record the pick with its model, settings and seed, and pin it.
- **Try the pick inside the approved sound** before committing: the same proof mix with the new voice, checking
  loudness and a Whisper read.
- **Brand words decide close calls.** One engine clipped the brand's name on the first film; the best current model said
  it in full. Put every brand word in the lexicon so the checks listen for it.
- **Time shots from the real reads.** A deliberate narrator can read 1.5 to 3.2 words a second; the shots are re-timed
  from the takes after voicing.

## Which engine and model

- Narration runs on ElevenLabs directly, on its best model (recorded in `registry.json`, pinned per film). A generation
  vendor's own TTS route gave lower bitrate, allowed only a few jobs at once, and clipped a brand word.
- For long reads (60 to 120 seconds of continuous narration), A/B the best model against the vendor's most stable
  long-form model before choosing.
- For pieces with several voices, the vendor's dialogue endpoint takes requests up to about 2,000 characters, any number
  of speakers, and previous and next context.
- Check the best models against the live API at the start of a project; the catalogue changes.

# Approvals: sittings, packets and the owner's yes

People judge what machines can't: the look, the voice, the sound, the hero moments and the final cut. Slate's job is to
put the right thing in front of them at the right time, record their decision against the exact bytes they judged, and
never mistake anything else for a yes.

## The two sittings (they block)

| Sitting | What it approves | What you prepare |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-production** | the checklist of asks, the claims, the script, the voice shortlist, and the look test when the brand's look isn't approved yet | GOAL.md with every ask; the truth pack and the claims list; SCRIPT.md; a casting reel (slate-voice); a moving 10 to 15 second look test with sound (slate-motion) |
| **Final cut** | the film itself (in express mode, everything above too) | the review packet (`slate review`): the phone cut, the contact sheet, what changed, open questions; every gate's status |

At a sitting: finish the packet, say plainly what's waiting for them and why, and stop. Don't start the next stage
"to save time"; it will be rebuilt if they change their mind.

## Packets (they don't block)

Hero moments, generated takes, sound proofs, voice takes and score takes go into review packets the owner answers when
they like. Keep working on everything that doesn't depend on them. When they answer, record it.

## What an approval is

- **Bound to exact bytes.** Record each approval with the command `slate status` names for that stage. It stores the
  SHA-256 of the file approved, who approved it and their words. Change the file and it's no longer approved.
- **Kinds Slate records:** checklist, claims, script, voice shortlist, look test, final cut (the sittings); hero,
  plate, sound proof, take, score take (packets); and spend (a yes to spend again on something already paid for).
- **Locks follow.** Approved takes, score takes, plates and the final cut are locked by content hash. Regenerating one
  needs an explicit force and a recorded spend approval.
- **Only a person approves.** Never record an approval on someone's behalf, never read approval into silence or a
  thumbs-up on something else, and never treat a REVIEW gate as a pass.
- **By ear and by eye.** Voices, sound and looks are chosen by the owner listening and watching. Measurements shortlist
  and catch faults; they never decide.

## Human approval points across a production

1. The goal and its checklist, in the requester's words.
2. The source of truth for 
[… 4,347 characters left out of the recording …]
rs' exported beats;
- a separate, timeboxed track for any alternative approach being tested;
- finals and sound done centrally, one at a time, never by the builders.

Research can be delegated the same way (if you can run sub-agents; otherwise do it in turn): a character's philosophy
into a voice brief, a motion spec from real references, a capability brief where every line carries a source. Every
delegated brief says what to return and where every claim came from.

## Choosing the production route

Before building, compare the candidate routes for the film (built in code with the Remotion kit, built in After
Effects, the open web renderer, generation for real-world shots), recommend one, and timebox a test of the strongest
alternative if it's a close call. Record the choice and the owner's approval. The engine can be chosen per brand or per
act during look development.

## One clock

Every beat is keyed to the voice's words, and picture and sound read the same resolved timeline. So a full re-voice
re-times the film automatically; the renders and the mix still have to be rebuilt, and `slate make <target>` rebuilds
only what's stale, in order. `slate make all` goes through to delivery; `slate make --list` shows each node's state
without running anything.

## Keeping intention across parallel versions

Intentionality degrades when several films or acts are built at once. Tie every move to a word or an idea, prefer fewer
and better moves, and judge new work against the best earlier film's code and notes. Hold masters until the pass is
done.

## Machines

- Render locally, one heavy job at a time, through the queue. Never on a borrowed machine or the owner's work computer.
- Too much parallel rendering thrashes a Mac: six builders plus finals once drove the load to 293 on 14 cores. The
  queue's per-resource locks and its load guard exist for this.
- Keep heavy media out of cloud-synced folders; films live in `~/Movies/Slate/` by default for that reason.
- Never edit a shell script while a job is running it (zsh reads scripts incrementally).
- One copy of any MCP client at a time: two copies ran every action twice.

## Evaluating a suggested tool

When someone suggests a library, an MCP server or a skill, check it quickly and record the verdict with reasons: does
the repository exist, does it do what it claims, does it write files or only play live, would it open a browser, does
it need system permissions (those installs go to the owner)? See dependencies.md.
